title: Cost I: The Value Chain and Structural Cost Advantage
keyQuestion: How does a firm get a structural cost advantage?

reading.name: The Value Chain (brief): 'A pizza that costs five dollars'

case.name: Aldi: Focused Discounter or Broad Cost Leader? ('The Machine Behind the Lowest Price')

slides: S7 deck 'Structural Cost Advantage' (25): five sources of cost advantage, value chain walk-through with Little Caesars, examples by activity. Aldi price index and cost-gap waterfall are at the start of the S8 deck (slides 2-3). PROVA Case Quiz 2: where Aldi's price gap comes from and what kind of advantage it creates.

framework.name: Porter's value chain (as an analysis, not a diagram)
framework.summary: A firm has no costs; activities have costs. A firm is a collection of discrete activities and wins or loses in each separately. Nine generic categories — five primary (touch the product on its way to the buyer) and four support — with margin as what's left when WTP exceeds the cost of everything to its left. The boxes are a starting point; advantage often sits between them (linkages).

components.name: Primary activities
components.what: Inbound logistics, operations, outbound logistics, marketing & sales, service.

components.name: Support activities
components.what: Procurement, technology development, human resource management, firm infrastructure — they make primary activities possible and run across all of them.

components.name: Split until the economics differ
components.what: Porter's nine are generic on purpose. Keep splitting while parts have different cost drivers, assets or effects on WTP ('operations' at an airline: gate turnaround vs. engine overhaul). If every activity has the same cost driver, you haven't cut finely enough.

components.name: Linkages
components.what: When the cost or effectiveness of one activity depends on how another is performed (more inbound inspection → less rework). The least-used part of the framework and why chains are hard to copy: a rival can observe activities but not which subsidizes which (Amazon's 2023 regionalization took $0.45+ per unit out with no single activity getting cheaper).

components.name: Five-step analysis
components.what: 1) Disaggregate until activities have different economics. 2) Put a cost AND an asset against every box. 3) Ask what drives cost in each box (Porter's ten drivers). 4) Work the linkages, not the boxes (including suppliers' and channels' chains). 5) Decide what to own, buy, or let someone else's brand ride on.

components.name: Porter's ten cost drivers
components.what: Scale, learning, capacity utilization, linkages, interrelationships across business units, vertical integration, timing of entry, discretionary policy choices, location, institutional factors (regulation, union status).

components.name: Deleting an activity
components.what: The most reliable cost reduction, because performing an activity more cheaply invites the rival to respond (Little Caesars: no order-taking, no drivers, no counter at the Portal).

components.name: Own one link
components.what: Perform one activity so far beyond anyone that the industry must come to you: ASML (inbound; only EUV maker), TSMC and YKK (operations), Amazon (outbound; 6.7B US parcels), Ritz-Carlton (service).

components.name: Profit pools
components.what: Total profit earned at every point along an industry's chain; profit concentration differs from revenue concentration. Value chain = efficiency instrument (your ledger); profit pool = positioning instrument (industry filings). Four steps (Gadiesh & Gilbert): define boundaries, size the pool, estimate each activity's share, reconcile. Draw revenue share on x, operating margin on y.

components.name: Five sources of cost advantage (slides)
components.what: Lower input costs; economies of scale or scope; learning and experience; proprietary knowledge; different business models (eliminating steps or performing new activities).

terms.def: The sequence of activities a firm performs to turn inputs into a product sold to a buyer; Porter's nine generic categories plus margin.
A dependency in which the cost or effectiveness of one activity depends on how another is performed.
A cost position that is a consequence of a system of choices (business-model design) rather than a cost-cutting program, which is why rivals who copy one element get nothing.
Cost advantage that comes from NOT performing an activity (no service departments, no advertising, no delivery); it disappears the moment breadth obliges the firm to perform it.
Cost advantage from volume (procurement leverage) or superior productivity (cut-case pallets, multi-face barcodes); tends to travel, even compound, as scope widens.
The total profit earned at every point along an industry's value chain.
Information that is not public and is viewed as the property of the holder (patents; hard-to-replicate processes).
Via bargaining power (Walmart), cooperation with suppliers (Toyota), location (Nike), preferred access to inputs (Saudi conventional oil at $5.40 vs. Alberta oil sands at $72).

claims.claim: A five-dollar pizza is not the result of one clever purchasing decision; it is a chain of about a dozen activities each designed to cost less — one of which, the delivery driver, was deleted.

Little Caesars linkage: made-ahead production only works with a narrow menu; a narrow menu only works at a low price; a low price only works with high throughput per labor hour, which made-ahead production delivers. Pull one out and the others stop making sense.

A value chain analysis tells you where the cost went out; it does not tell you who kept it. Ask both (Little Caesars' savings were partly captured by the franchisor: 11% fee load vs. Domino's 9.5%, $446.5k minimum buildout vs. $107.5k, mandatory Blue Line supply).
A low-cost position that does not also deliver volume is fragile (Little Caesars ~$950k AUV vs. Domino's $1,385k — the opposite of Walmart's low cost + high throughput).

The diagnostic question for Aldi: where in the value chain does the cost advantage come from, which links depend on scale, which on refusal, and which would breadth put at risk? The scaling debate turns on the composition of the gap.

If most of Aldi's gap sits in links that scale (procurement, operations, private label), broad cost leadership is the natural continuation; if a large share sits in refusals, 'scaling up' is the slow disassembly of the machine.

Domino's and Little Caesars have the same vertical integration with opposite governance: Domino's franchisees aren't required to buy from its supply chain and get 50% of its profit; Little Caesars mandates Blue Line.
The profit pool question is not 'how do we perform this activity better?' but 'are we standing in the right part of the chain at all?'

failures.name: Not cutting finely enough
failures.what: Boxes with the same cost driver hide the analysis.

failures.name: Cost without assets
failures.what: An activity cheap to run but heavy in working capital is not cheap.

failures.name: Assuming scale is the answer
failures.what: Go through all ten drivers; cost may be a 1998 policy choice.

failures.name: Local optimization
failures.what: Savings that push cost downstream into another activity or partner's budget.

failures.name: Accidental make-or-buy
failures.what: Activities performed only because they always have been.

failures.name: Ignoring who keeps the savings
failures.what: Cost removed by the chain can be captured by the franchisor, a supplier or a channel.

failures.name: Drift from refusal
failures.what: For a refusal-based cost leader, every reasonable-sounding addition (delivery, digital, wider range, bigger boxes) re-adds cost; enough of them and the firm is stuck in the middle.

caseFacts.fact: Aldi carries ~1,400-2,000 items vs. 30,000-40,000+ at a conventional supermarket; ~90% private label (vs. ~20-25%); ~12,000 sq ft selling area (vs. 40,000-60,000); 3-5 staff per shift (vs. 15-50+); price often ~15-40% below.
caseFacts.why: The assortment decision cascades: volume per SKU → bargaining power; less space and labor; faster turns; tractable quality control. Exhibit 4 is labeled directional.

caseFacts.fact: Professor's anchor: Consumer Reports price index (late 2025, published April 2026) — Aldi 91.7, Walmart 100, Kroger 114.8, Trader Joe's 124.6, Whole Foods 139.7. Aldi vs. Kroger = 79.9 → a ~20.1-point gap.
caseFacts.why: The observed price gap the value-chain build must explain. (Aldi's own study claims 36%, but that compares its private label to national brands; like-for-like vs. competitor private label is 22%.)

caseFacts.fact: Professor's waterfall from conventional = 100: assortment −2.5, private label −5, logistics −1.5, real estate −1.5, store labor −5, replenishment −0.75, front end −0.75, shrink −1.25, marketing −0.75, overhead −0.75, customer-borne −0.45 → Aldi ≈ 80. Built total 20.2 vs. observed 20.1.
caseFacts.why: Private label and store labor are half the total and both trace to the assortment decision. The match is a plausibility check, not an independent validation; the benchmark slides behind each bar are not in the export.

caseFacts.fact: Value-chain mapping in the case: procurement = scale/bargaining; inbound logistics = process/scale; operations = process (highest labor productivity); outbound/delivery = refusal now partly re-added; marketing & sales = refusal; service = refusal (double guarantee substitutes for service staff); HR = process/culture (above-market wages on lean staffing); technology = refusal now partly re-added; infrastructure = structure/culture (private, debt-light, thin HQ).
caseFacts.why: Exhibit 3 worksheet: estimate each link's share of the gap and whether it survives breadth.

caseFacts.fact: Growth: 180+ new stores in 2026, Maine 40th state, Colorado 50+ stores, $9B plan to reach 3,200 stores by 2028 (from ~2,800); 1 in 3 US households shopped Aldi; 17M new customers in 2025; ~400 Winn-Dixie/Harveys stores acquired (200+ conversions by 2027); Instacart/DoorDash/Uber Eats delivery; 2026 digital storefront.
caseFacts.why: The scope question: each addition is either the transition to broad cost leadership or drift.

caseFacts.fact: Limited SKUs cover ~90% of a typical household's annual purchases; award-winning private label attracts affluent shoppers by choice — but 'one in three households' measures visits, not loyalty (often a secondary split-basket stop).
caseFacts.why: Evidence on both sides of 'will it scale?' (Exhibit 6 deliberately gives neither column the last word).

caseFacts.fact: Porter paper: Aldi holds roughly 3% of US grocery spending despite decades of lowest prices — the market's estimate of what the deleted conveniences were worth.
caseFacts.why: Cost leaders must hold parity on what buyers care about; refusal has a demand cost.

caseFacts.fact: Little Caesars: carryout only 1959-2019; Hot-N-Ready $5 from 2004 to Jan 2022 ($5.55; now ~$6.79); Pizza Portal 2018; Blue Line purchases $1.64B (FY2021); ACSI 78 vs. industry 79; net US units +93 in 2025 in a shrinking category.
caseFacts.why: The brief's worked example of building a cost position activity by activity — and its limits.

strongAnalysis: Answer the Key Question: a structural cost advantage comes from an interlocking system of activity choices — what you delete, what you simplify, how activities link — not from a cost-cutting program or size. It is hard to copy because rivals can see individual activities but not the linkages, and copying one element gets them nothing (Porter §3; VC linkages).

Aldi's gap, link by link (professor's waterfall): about half from private label (5) and store labor (5), both downstream of the limited-assortment choice; assortment itself 2.5; logistics and real estate 1.5 each; shrink 1.25; replenishment, front end, marketing, overhead 0.75 each; customer-borne (bagging, carts) 0.45.

Classify each link: scale/process links (procurement, private label, logistics, store operations) travel and compound with breadth; refusal links (marketing, service, delivery, technology, customer-borne work) disappear when breadth forces the activity back in. By the professor's numbers the refusal-type links (marketing 0.75, customer-borne 0.45, parts of front end/overhead) are a modest share, which supports 'the machine can scale' — IF Aldi keeps assortment narrow, since assortment drives the two biggest bars.

What kind of advantage: a structural (business-model) cost advantage, not primarily a scale advantage — 'a single store embodies most of the advantage' (S8 synthesis). That is why big grocers don't just copy it: the trade-offs (fewer SKUs, no services) would destroy their own WTP and model.

Recommendation logic: grow broad in footprint while staying narrow in assortment and refusals (Costco/Southwest precedent); treat second sizes, delivery economics and larger converted boxes as taxes to be priced against each bar of the waterfall.

counter.argument: Aldi's advantage is really scale and bargaining power — with ~13,000 stores worldwide and enormous volume per SKU, it's a buying-power story, so any big grocer (Walmart, Kroger) could match it.
counter.response: Volume per SKU comes from the assortment decision, not company size: Walmart is far bigger and still priced above Aldi (100 vs. 91.7). The professor's waterfall puts most of the gap in private label and store labor that follow from limited assortment and the no-frills operating system. Big grocers can't match it without abandoning the 30,000-SKU, service-rich model their customers pay for — the trade-off is the barrier.

courseMap.text: Generic strategy chooses which half of the wedge leads; the value chain is where a cost position is actually built activity by activity (Porter §9). Next: scale and learning (S8) are two of the ten cost drivers; profit pools connect back to industry structure (S4).

slideExtras.topic: Little Caesars on the value chain
slideExtras.detail: Inbound: bulk purchasing, centralized/owned distribution, proximity, efficient transport, fewer SKUs, bargaining power. Operations: simple menu, Hot-N-Ready, no dine-in infrastructure, labor costs, in-house dough and sauce, measured toppings, real estate strategy. Outbound: Pizza Portal. Marketing: $205M ad spend vs. Pizza Hut $100M and Domino's $33M (as shown on slide).

Firm infrastructure: Allegiant (Provo), WGU (no campus), Costco (centralized decisions, few promotions), Ryanair (one aircraft type). HR: Costco low turnover, McDonald's task modularization, Southwest cross-training, Little Caesars plans on churn, Toyota workers solve problems. Technology: Netflix recommendations, Walmart Retail Link, Uber dispatch, Little Giant ladder design. Procurement: Toyota keiretsu, Walmart negotiation, Costco very few SKUs.
Eliminating steps: Zara (cut long forecasting cycles), Warby Parker (cut physical retail). Performing new activities: Netflix streaming, Aldi customers bag groceries, Uber matching.

Aldi = structural cost advantage (business-model design; scale-dependence modest — a single store embodies most of it; barrier = incumbents' unwillingness to accept the trade-offs; leaks via model drift and rivals copying the format). Netflix = economies of scale (fixed content cost over subscribers; essential scale; barrier = years of losses and a rising ante; leaks via suppliers repricing, talent rents, basis of competition shifting).
